short.headline: India’s median age is climbing from 21 to 48 by 2100
short.dek: In 2000, half the country was under 21. By 2100, that midpoint is projected to hit 47.8 years, signalling a historic transformation.
short.body: Twenty-five years ago, India was a young country. The median age was 21.2 years. Today, that figure has already risen and is climbing faster. The share of children has shrunk from over 40% in 1960 to less than 25% now. The working-age share has bulged to 68%, but it will peak soon. Meanwhile, the elderly are the fastest-growing group: from 3.3% in 1960 to 7.1% now, and headed much higher. Falling birth rates and longer lives drive this shift. India is getting older, and the speed of that change will challenge everything from pensions to primary schools. But there is also opportunity in a large working-age population today, if jobs keep pace.

macha.heading: Bhai, what does all this age data actually mean?
macha.body: Think of India like a joint family that is suddenly having fewer kids and the elders are living longer. For decades, we had many young people and relatively few old. Now the balance is shifting. The median age — the age where half the country is younger — has already crossed 30, and it is heading past 40 in this century. This means less pressure on schools but more need for hospitals and pensions. The big bulge of people in their 20s and 30s today is a once-in-a-generation advantage — if we can create enough decent jobs for them. But it will not last forever. The window is closing as the bulge moves into old age. So age is not just a number; it is a clock.
macha.soWhat: India's youth bulge is turning into an elderly bulge. The time to build systems for both is now.

article.title: How old is India? Tracking a population's long march from 21 to 48
article.standfirst: Half of India was under 21 in 2000. By 2100, half could be older than 48, a shift that will reshape families, work, and care. These eight charts explain the numbers.
article.bodyMarkdown:
## What is India's median age and how fast is it rising?

The median age is the age that splits the population into two equal halves: half the people are younger, half are older. In 2000, India's median age was 21.2 years. Imagine lining up all Indians from youngest to oldest. The person standing exactly in the middle would have just turned 21. By 2100, the United Nations projects that middle person will be 47.8 years old. That is a rise of more than 26 years over a century. The line chart tracks this climb. It is slow at first, then picks up speed as fewer children are born and older adults live longer. The median age is the single clearest number for how old a country is. It hides the full story of who is young and who is old, but it gives the headline: India is ageing, and the pace is about to accelerate.

## What does India's age pyramid look like in 2025?

A population pyramid shows the number of males and females in each five-year age band. The pyramid for 2025 is a projection, based on the United Nations' medium variant. Its shape is neither the classic wide-bottom pyramid of a young country nor the narrow base of an old one. Instead, it has a bulge in the young adult years. The largest cohorts are in their late 20s and early 20s. For example, the 25-29 age group is projected to be 12.9 crore strong, and the 20-24 group 12.5 crore. Meanwhile, the base is narrowing: the 0-4 category is projected at 11.1 crore. This is the echo of falling birth rates. At the top, the pyramid tapers, but women outlive men, so the bars on the female side are longer in the oldest ages. The pyramid captures a moment of transition, a one-time bulge of working-age people that will eventually become a bulge of elderly citizens.

## How have the shares of children, working-age, and elderly changed since 1960?

In 1960, children aged 0-14 made up 40.6% of India's population. By 2024, that share had dropped to 24.6%. The working-age group, 15-64, rose from 56.1% to 68.2% over the same period. The elderly, 65 and above, climbed from just 3.3% to 7.1%. These three lines on the chart tell the story of India's demographic transition. First, as fewer infants died, the working-age share began to swell. Then, as families had fewer children, the child share shrank fast. The working-age share is now near its peak. The elderly share, though still small, is growing faster than any other group. This shift does not happen evenly; the child share fell most steeply after the 1980s, while the working-age share rose until the 2010s and is now beginning to flatten. The elderly share will accelerate in the coming decades as the large adult cohorts grow old.

## What is the current age structure of India in broad life stages?

A snapshot for 2024 puts the three life stages in sharp relief: children 0-14 account for 24.6% of the population, the working-age 15-64 account for 68.2%, and older adults 65 and above account for 7.1%. In everyday terms, for every 100 Indians, about 25 are children, 68 are of typical working age, and 7 are elderly. This pie or stacked bar hides nuances, the working-age group includes teenagers still in school and people in their 60s nearing retirement. It also does not tell us how many of those working-age people actually work. So while the headline looks like a favourable ratio, the real dependency burden depends on labour force participation and productivity. The chart's simplicity is its strength: it shows at a glance that India is still demographically young but that the share of elderly is set to rise quickly as the working-age share peaks.

## How many older adults does each 100 working-age adults support?

The old-age dependency ratio measures the number of people aged 65 and older for every 100 people of working age (15-64). In 2000, that ratio was 7.35. By 2030, it is projected to reach 12.39. So in three decades, the number of elderly each 100 can potentially support has nearly doubled. The line chart shows a steady upward curve. A higher ratio means a heavier economic burden, at least on paper. But the ratio assumes everyone 15-64 is in the labour force, which is far from reality. Many women do not work outside the home, and many young people are studying. So the effective support ratio is even tighter. As the large cohorts now in their 30s move into old age, the ratio will worsen sharply after 2040. This chart is a warning: the window to prepare social security and healthcare for an ageing society is not as wide as it seems.

## How has the child dependency ratio changed?

The child dependency ratio is the mirror image: children aged 0-14 per 100 working-age people. In 2000, it was 59.22. By 2030, it will likely fall to 32.42. That is a dramatic decline. A falling child ratio means that, in theory, each working-age adult has fewer children to raise and educate. For a family, it means more resources per child. For the government, it means a chance to invest more heavily in each child's health and schooling, rather than spreading too thinly. But the declining child ratio also means a smaller future workforce. The children of today are the workers of tomorrow. A child ratio that keeps falling eventually translates into a shrinking working-age population, which can slow economic growth. The line chart shows the drop levelling off; the ratio is not falling as fast as it once did, a sign that India's fertility decline may be stabilizing at a lower level.

## How has life expectancy at birth changed, and what does it mean for India's age?

Life expectancy at birth is the number of years a newborn would live if current death rates at each age stayed the same throughout their life. In 2000, an Indian newborn could expect 62.8 years. By 2030, that figure is projected to rise to 73.6 years. Women live longer: female life expectancy in 2030 is projected at 75.4 years, male at 72.0 years. Longer lives are the other half of the ageing story, alongside fewer births. When people survive to old age in greater numbers, the share of the population that is elderly grows. The line chart shows steady improvement, with a noticeable gap opening between women and men. This improvement reflects better nutrition, sanitation, immunisation, and healthcare. But it also means India will have more older people needing long-term care, pensions, and healthcare systems that are still designed for a younger population.

## How many more years can a 60-year-old expect to live?

Life expectancy at age 60 tells us the average number of additional years a person can expect after reaching that milestone. In 2021, a 60-year-old Indian could expect to live another 15.6 years, on average. Women at 60 could expect 16.5 more years, men 14.8. These numbers from the WHO give a clearer picture of ageing than life expectancy at birth, because they focus on the years that really swell the elderly population. The preciousness of these added years depends on health; living longer is a triumph, but it raises questions about the quality of those years. The 2021 data may have been depressed by the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2019, before the pandemic, the figures were higher: 18.5 years for both sexes combined. The chart shows that despite temporary shocks, the long trend is upward. Every extra year at age 60 adds to the growing queue of Indians entering old age, reshaping families and demanding new social arrangements.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The age that splits the population into two equal halves. Picture a line with every Indian sorted from youngest to oldest; the person exactly in the middle sets the median age. It is not the average — it is the midpoint. So if the median age is 30, half the country is younger than 30 and half is older.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: It is the most direct answer to 'how old is India?' and the number driving the page.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A back-to-back horizontal bar chart showing the number of males and females in each age group, with the youngest at the bottom and oldest at the top. The shape tells you if a population is young (wide base, narrow top) or old (narrow base, wide middle).
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: It reveals the full age-and-sex structure behind a single median number.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A simple measure of economic burden: it counts how many dependents (young or old) there are for every 100 people of working age. It assumes that working-age people support the rest, even though many do not work.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: It translates age structure into a rough sense of how many hands are available to support non-working age groups.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Specifically, the number of people aged 65 and older for every 100 people aged 15-64. When this ratio rises, it means there are more elderly for each person of typical working age.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: It isolates the pressure that an ageing population places on workers and on retirement and healthcare systems.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The number of children aged 0-14 for every 100 people aged 15-64. A falling ratio means fewer children for each working-age adult.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: It tracks the declining burden of raising children as families have fewer kids, freeing resources for investment per child.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The average number of years a newborn baby would live if the death rates at each age stayed the same throughout their life. It is a snapshot of today's mortality conditions, not a forecast for a real baby.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Rising life expectancy is the main reason the elderly share is growing: fewer people die young and more survive into old age.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The average additional number of years a 60-year-old would live if current death rates persisted. It tells you how long people are living after they cross the traditional retirement threshold.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: It directly influences the size of the elderly population — the longer people live after 60, the larger the 65+ share becomes.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A calculation of future population based on assumptions about fertility, mortality, and migration. It is a 'what-if' scenario, not a prediction. Different assumptions produce different projections.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: All future numbers on this page — median age in 2100, the 2030 age structure — are projections. The actual path will depend on how birth and death rates evolve.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: In dependency ratios, this is conventionally defined as everyone aged 15 to 64. It does not mean everyone in this age group actually works; many are in school, unemployed, or engaged in unpaid domestic work.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: All dependency calculations use this group in the denominator, so the true economic burden may be higher if many working-age people are not earning.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The shift from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as a country develops. In the middle of the transition, the working-age share gets a temporary boost — the 'demographic dividend' — before ageing sets in.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: India is midway through this transition, explaining why the child share is falling and the elderly share is poised to accelerate.

visualizationDecisions.reason: A line chart over two decades shows the steady climb and allows mobile readers to grasp the long trend easily.
A pyramid is the only clear way to show age and sex together; on mobile, labels must be kept short for readability.
Three lines in one view let readers compare the shares; sparse ticks keep it mobile-friendly.
A share strip or stacked bar conveys composition clearly without clutter on small screens.
A line with prominent labels shows the rise clearly and is easily read on a phone.
Similar to old-age dependency, a clean line chart efficiently communicates the decline.
A multi-line (male/female/total) chart shows the gap without overwhelming mobile screens.
A focused window reveals recent trends and pandemic impacts cleanly on mobile.

chartExplainers.title: India's median age, 2000 to 2030
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's median age has risen from 21.2 years in 2000 and is projected to continue climbing steadily.
chartExplainers.detail: This line chart tracks the median age — the age that splits the population in half — from 2000 to 2030. In 2000, the median was 21.2 years; a typical Indian was just old enough to vote. By 2030, the line has risen significantly, reflecting falling birth rates and longer lives. The climb is gradual at first but picks up pace after 2015. The trend reveals a country that is rapidly leaving its youth behind. Every year the median inches higher, the centre of gravity shifts towards middle age. The chart uses United Nations projections, so the future path assumes current trends in fertility and mortality will continue.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It is the single clearest number for answering how old India is.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read the line from left to right; the steeper the line, the faster the ageing.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not confuse median age with average age — the median is less sensitive to very old or very young outliers.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Keep the y-axis short and use large year labels at sparse intervals.

chartExplainers.title: Age pyramid, 2025
chartExplainers.takeaway: India in 2025 has a bulge of young adults in their 20s and a narrowing base of children.
chartExplainers.detail: This population pyramid shows the projected number of males and females in each five-year age band for 2025. The shape is a transitional pyramid: not the wide-base pyramid of a young country, nor the narrow-base inverted pyramid of an old one. The largest bars are in the 20s, with the 25-29 group at about 12.9 crore and the 20-24 group at 12.5 crore. The base is shrinking: children aged 0-4 are projected to be 11.1 crore. At older ages, women outlive men, so the female bars extend further. This pyramid captures the demographic dividend — a one-time bulge of working-age people — that will shape India's economy for the next two decades.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It reveals the full age-and-sex distribution that a single median number cannot show.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Horizontal bars extend left for males and right for females; the youngest are at the bottom. The shape tells you if the population is young or old.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not mistake the length of the bars for absolute numbers unless the axes are labelled with counts.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Keep bar labels short; use abbreviations like 'M' and 'F' for sexes.

chartExplainers.title: How India's age mix has shifted
chartExplainers.takeaway: The share of children has nearly halved since 1960, while the working-age share has swollen and the elderly share has begun a long rise.
chartExplainers.detail: Three lines track the proportion of the population in three broad age groups from 1960 to 2024. The child share (0-14) dropped from 40.6% to 24.6%. The working-age share (15-64) surged from 56.1% to 68.2%. The elderly share (65+) more than doubled from 3.3% to 7.1%. The lines show a classic demographic transition. The child share fell most steeply after the 1980s as families had fewer children. The working-age share peaked around 2020 and will soon decline. The elderly share, though still small, is accelerating. This chart makes the ageing process concrete: the same population that once had four out of ten as children now has just one in four.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It shows that ageing is not one trend but three shares moving together.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Watch how the three lines diverge: the child line falls, the working-age line rises then flattens, the elderly line rises slowly now but will accelerate.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume the three shares sum to 100% without checking axis labels — they do, but always verify.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use only three colours and label each line directly on the chart.

chartExplainers.title: Age structure today
chartExplainers.takeaway: In 2024, nearly seven out of ten Indians are of working age, while one in four is a child and one in fourteen is elderly.
chartExplainers.detail: A simple pie or stacked bar shows the population split into three life stages for the latest year. Children (0-14) make up 24.6%, working-age adults (15-64) 68.2%, and older adults (65+) 7.1%. For every 100 people, roughly 25 are children, 68 are of typical working age, and 7 are elderly. This snapshot makes the age structure intuitive. But the broad categories hide important details: the working-age group includes teenagers and young adults still in education, as well as near-retirees. And the elderly share, though small, will swell rapidly as the large working-age cohort ages. This chart is a quick health check on the population’s current composition.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It gives an instant, intuitive picture of the population split into life stages.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Look at the size of each segment; the largest is working-age, which means a potential dividend.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't assume every person in the working-age group actually works; many are not in the labour force.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use a horizontal stacked bar or three clearly labelled segments.

chartExplainers.title: Old-age dependency ratio
chartExplainers.takeaway: The number of elderly per 100 working-age adults nearly doubled from 7.35 in 2000 to a projected 12.39 in 2030.
chartExplainers.detail: This line chart plots the old-age dependency ratio — the count of people 65 and older for every 100 people aged 15-64. In 2000, the ratio was 7.35. By 2030, it reaches 12.39. That means the support burden from the elderly has intensified sharply in three decades. The line curves upward steadily, and the rise will steepen after 2040 as the large cohorts born in the 1970s and 1980s enter old age. This ratio is a rough measure of economic pressure on workers and social systems. It assumes everyone 15-64 is a worker, which is not true — many are students or homemakers. So the actual strain on those who do work is even greater. This chart is an early warning that India's pension, health, and care systems have little time to prepare.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It directly quantifies the economic weight of an ageing population.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A rising line means more elderly per 100 working-age; a higher number signals a growing economic burden.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read the ratio as a statement about actual workers — many working-age people are not employed.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use a bold line with large labels for the start and end years.

chartExplainers.title: Child dependency ratio
chartExplainers.takeaway: The child dependency ratio fell from 59.2 per 100 working-age in 2000 to a projected 32.4 in 2030, cutting the burden of raising children almost in half.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart shows the child dependency ratio — children aged 0-14 per 100 people of working age. The drop is steep: from 59.22 in 2000 to 32.42 in 2030. For every 100 working-age adults, the number of children they might support fell by 27 in three decades. That is a huge release of resources. Families can spend more on each child, and governments can invest more in education and health per child. But a falling child ratio also means a smaller future workforce. The children of today are the workers of tomorrow; fewer children now will eventually mean fewer workers in 20 years. The line chart shows the decline levelling off, suggesting that India's fertility may be stabilizing.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It captures the youth side of the dependency equation and shows why investment per child can rise.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A falling line means fewer dependents per working-age adult, which normally signals a demographic dividend.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: A falling child ratio does not automatically mean less spending on children; per-child investment often increases.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use a single descending line with annotations for the key years.

chartExplainers.title: Life expectancy at birth
chartExplainers.takeaway: Life expectancy at birth jumped from 62.8 years in 2000 to a projected 73.6 years in 2030, with women living about three years longer than men.
chartExplainers.detail: Life expectancy at birth summarises the average lifespan a newborn would have if current death rates persist. In 2000, it was 62.8 years. By 2030, it is projected to reach 73.6 years — a gain of nearly 11 years in just three decades. The chart shows separate lines for females and males. Women consistently outlive men: in 2030, female life expectancy is projected at 75.4 years, male at 72.0 years. This steady rise drives the ageing of the population: fewer people die young, and more survive to old age. Better nutrition, immunisation, and medical care all play a role. For a family, it means grandparents are around longer. For the country, it means a growing cohort of older people who will need income, care, and dignity in their later years.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Longer lives are one of the two engines of population ageing, alongside falling fertility.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Rising lines mean longer lifespans; the gap between male and female lines shows the sex difference.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Life expectancy is not a prediction of how long any specific child will live — it is a summary of current mortality rates.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use two or three lines with a shared legend and keep y-axis ticks sparse.

chartExplainers.title: Life expectancy at 60
chartExplainers.takeaway: In 2021, a 60-year-old could expect 15.6 more years of life, with women getting 16.5 years and men 14.8 years.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart shows life expectancy at age 60 from the WHO. It tells us how many additional years a person who reaches 60 can expect, on average, using current death rates. In 2021, the figure for both sexes was 15.6 years. Women at 60 could expect 16.5 more years, men 14.8. The long trend has been upward, though the pandemic caused a dip. In 2019, the combined figure was 18.5 years. Every additional year at age 60 directly adds to the elderly population. This remaining lifespan is crucial for planning retirement, healthcare, and family support. As this number grows, the idea of 'old age' itself shifts — being 60 is no longer the end of active life for many.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It isolates the number of years that directly swell the elderly population after age 60.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Rising lines mean longer lives for those who reach 60; check the gap between males and females.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: These are period life expectancies, not forecasts for a current 60-year-old; they assume today's death rates remain constant.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Show a short time window like 2010-2021 with clear labels.

sectionPlan.heading: How have the shares of children, working-age, and elderly changed since 1960?
sectionPlan.job: Trace the decline in child share from 40.6% in 1960 to 24.6% in 2024, the rise in working-age share from 56.1% to 68.2%, and the increase in elderly share from 3.3% to 7.1%.
lockedNumbersToUse: Population ages 0-14, earliest (40.6%)
Population ages 0-14, latest (24.6%)
Population ages 15-64, earliest (56.1%)
Population ages 15-64, latest (68.2%)
Population ages 65 and above, earliest (3.3%)
Population ages 65 and above, latest (7.1%)
sectionPlan.caveat: These percentages are from World Bank data; the UN may produce slightly different estimates.

sectionPlan.heading: What is the current age structure of India in broad life stages?
sectionPlan.job: Show a simplified breakdown: children (0-14), working-age (15-64), and elderly (65+) as shares of total population in the latest year (2024).
lockedNumbersToUse: Population ages 0-14, latest (24.6%)
Population ages 15-64, latest (68.2%)
Population ages 65 and above, latest (7.1%)
sectionPlan.caveat: These broad groups hide variation within, like the large youth bulge.

sectionPlan.heading: How many older adults does each 100 working-age adults support?
sectionPlan.job: Explain the old-age dependency ratio, showing it rising from about 7.35 in 2000 to 12.39 in 2030 (for the 65+/15-64 ratio), and note that the ratio will worsen significantly by 2100.
lockedNumbersToUse: Old-age dependency ratio (Median, Both sexes, Not applicable): value (2000, 7.35)
Old-age dependency ratio (Median, Both sexes, Not applicable): value (2030, 12.39)
sectionPlan.caveat: This ratio assumes all working-age people are actually economically active; in reality, many are not.

sectionPlan.heading: How has the child dependency ratio changed?
sectionPlan.job: Show the child dependency ratio dropping from about 59.2 children per 100 working-age in 2000 to 32.4 in 2030, reflecting falling fertility.
lockedNumbersToUse: Child dependency ratio (Median, Both sexes, Not applicable): value (2000, 59.22)
Child dependency ratio (Median, Both sexes, Not applicable): value (2030, 32.42)
sectionPlan.caveat: A falling child dependency ratio reduces pressure on schools but eventually the same cohort will move into working-age.

sectionPlan.heading: How has life expectancy at birth changed, and what does it mean for India's age?
sectionPlan.job: Explain that longer lives drive ageing: life expectancy rose from 62.7 years in 2000 to 73.6 years in 2030 (projected), and show sex differences.

chartPlan.title: India's median age, 2000 to 2030
chartPlan.whyShowThis: This is the single clearest number for how old the country is.
chartPlan.howToRead: Trace the line from 2000 (21.2) to the latest year and then to 2030; the steepness shows the pace of ageing.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Don't confuse median age with average age — the median is the midpoint, less sensitive to very old or young outliers.

chartPlan.title: Age pyramid, 2025
chartPlan.whyShowThis: It reveals the full age-and-sex shape behind a single median number.
chartPlan.howToRead: Horizontal bars to the left are males, right are females; each bar is a 5-year age group. The shape shows whether the population is young or old.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Don't read a pyramid as a single number — it shows relative size of cohorts, not absolute counts unless labeled.

chartPlan.title: How India's age mix has shifted
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Ageing is really three shares moving at once: children, working-age, and older.
chartPlan.howToRead: Three lines over time: the child share falls, working-age rises then plateaus, older share rises slowly now but will accelerate.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Don't assume the shares sum to 100% only from these three groups; always check labels.

chartPlan.title: Age structure today
chartPlan.whyShowThis: A clean snapshot of the population split into life stages right now.
chartPlan.howToRead: A pie or stacked bar showing the proportion of children (0-14), working-age (15-64), and older (65+).
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Broad age groups can conceal the size of specific cohorts, like the large youth bulge.

chartPlan.title: Old-age dependency ratio
chartPlan.whyShowThis: It directly measures the economic burden of an ageing population on those of working age.
chartPlan.howToRead: The line shows the number of older adults (65+) per 100 people aged 15-64. Higher means more dependents per worker.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: This ratio assumes all 15-64 are working; many are students, unemployed, or homemakers.

chartPlan.title: Child dependency ratio
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The youth side of the dependency picture shows the declining burden of children.
chartPlan.howToRead: The line shows children (0-14) per 100 people aged 15-64. A falling ratio means fewer resources per child are needed in theory.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: A falling ratio doesn't automatically mean less spending on children; per-child investment may rise.

chartPlan.title: Life expectancy at birth
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Longer lives are half of why a population ages — alongside fewer births.
chartPlan.howToRead: Lines for total, male, female over time. Rising lines mean people are living longer on average.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Life expectancy does not predict how long a specific person will live; it's a summary of mortality patterns.

chartPlan.title: Life expectancy at 60
chartPlan.whyShowThis: It shows how many more years someone who reaches 60 can expect, which drives the size of the elderly population.
chartPlan.howToRead: Lines by sex; higher values mean older adults are living longer after retirement age.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: These are period life expectancies — they use current death rates, which can change.

visualizationDecisions.reason: A line chart over the full period shows the trend clearly and allows phone readers to see the long arc.
A pyramid is essential for age-sex structure; mobile-friendly if labels are kept short.

visualizationDecisions.indicatorOrVisual: How India's age mix has shifted
visualizationDecisions.reason: A multi-line chart lets readers compare the three shares in one view, with sparse ticks for mobile.
A share strip or stacked bar works well on mobile to show composition without clutter.
A line chart with large labels shows the rise clearly and is easily readable on mobile.
Similar to old-age dependency, a line chart efficiently shows the decline.
A line chart with male/female/total can show gaps without overwhelming mobile screens.
A line chart shows recent trends and pandemic impacts clearly; keep it focused on a window.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The age that splits the population into two equal halves — half the people are younger, half are older.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: It is the most direct answer to 'how old is India?' and rising quickly.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A back-to-back horizontal bar chart showing the number of males and females in each age group, youngest at the bottom.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: It reveals whether a population is young (wide base) or old (narrow base, wide middle).

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The number of dependents (young or old) per 100 people of working age. It assumes working-age people support others.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: It translates age structure into a rough measure of economic burden, showing how the ratio is shifting.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The number of people aged 65 and older for every 100 people aged 15-64.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: It isolates the burden of an ageing population on workers and pension systems.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The number of children aged 0-14 for every 100 people aged 15-64.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: It tracks the falling burden of children as fertility declines.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The average number of years a newborn would live if current death rates at each age remained the same throughout their life.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Rising life expectancy is the main reason the population is ageing — fewer people die young.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The average additional number of years a 60-year-old would live if current death rates persist.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: It shows how many years older adults are adding after age 60, swelling the elderly population.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A calculation of future population based on assumptions about fertility, mortality, and migration. It is not a forecast but a 'what if'.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: All future numbers (median age 2100, 2030 age structure) are projections, and they depend on the assumptions being correct.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The group defined as 15-64 years old, used in dependency ratios. It does not mean everyone in this group works.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: It is the denominator in dependency ratios, so understanding it prevents overestimating the economic burden.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The shift from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as a country develops, leading to an older population.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India is in the middle of this transition, explaining the falling child share and rising elderly share.

proseRules: No calculations unless the evidence packet supplies the derived number

selectionRules: Start from the page question, not from the indicator name.
Choose the smallest set of visuals that explains scale, trend, structure, comparison, and caveat.
Prefer mobile-friendly charts: line charts with sparse ticks, horizontal bars, share strips, pyramids only when essential, and no dense tables.
Use one strong pull quote only when the evidence supports it with a number.
Add glossary blocks for technical terms that normal readers may not know.
caveats: Use only figures present in lockedNumbers or sourceSummaries.
If a related theme indicator is present, you may use it for context, but do not pretend it is the main answer.
If source coverage is thin, say so directly.
Do not compare states, districts, or cities unless the evidence packet contains those geographies.
forbiddenClaims: Do not infer causality from a trend unless the evidence explicitly supports it.
Do not cite a source that is not present in sourceSummaries.
